> **How to read this file.** Section 3 runs the simulation, sections 4 and 5 show the evidence, and section 8 states my selected n. The reusable code lives in `R/functions.R`; this file only calls it. This is the one population where the CLT does not apply, so a few parts look different from the others.

## 1. Prediction

The Cauchy has such heavy tails that it has **no mean and no standard deviation**. The CLT needs a finite variance, so I predict it fails: averaging more observations will not make the sample mean more normal, and it will not even make it more concentrated. I predict that no sample size passes my rule.

## 2. The population

```{r}
#| label: setup
source("R/setup.R")
source("R/functions.R")

generator <- function(n) rcauchy(n, location = 0, scale = 1)
```

Cauchy(0, 1) has a bell-like center but extremely heavy tails. Its mean μ and standard deviation σ **do not exist** (the integrals diverge), so there is no theoretical standard error σ/√n to compare with. Two things I can say exactly:

- The **median is 0** and the middle half of the values lies between −1 and 1, so the interquartile range is 2.
- The average of n independent Cauchy(0, 1) values is **again exactly Cauchy(0, 1)**, for every n. Averaging does nothing to the shape.

```{r}
#| label: population-plot
#| fig-height: 3
curve(dcauchy(x), from = -8, to = 8, lwd = 3, col = "steelblue",
      main = "Cauchy(0, 1) population (black: normal for comparison)",
      xlab = "x", ylab = "density")
curve(dnorm(x), add = TRUE, lty = 2)
```

## 3. Simulation

For every sample size n in my list (`r min(n_values)` to `r max(n_values)`, `r length(n_values)` sizes), I draw B = `r format(B, big.mark = ",")` samples of n observations and keep each sample's mean. B is the number of repetitions; n is the size of each sample.

Because σ doesn't exist, I pass `NA` for the theoretical mean and SD. That makes the SD-ratio check impossible to pass, so my rule can never select an n. I add two measures that **do** exist for the Cauchy: the interquartile range (IQR) of the sample means, and the share of sample means beyond ±10.

```{r}
#| label: simulate
all_means <- simulate_all_n(generator, n_values)
results   <- summarize_means(all_means, NA, NA)
results$good <- flag_good(results)
n_star <- smallest_good_n(results)

results$median   <- apply(all_means, 2, median)
results$iqr      <- apply(all_means, 2, IQR)
results$beyond10 <- apply(all_means, 2, function(x) mean(abs(x) > 10))

dir.create("results", showWarnings = FALSE)
write.csv(results, "results/05_cauchy.csv", row.names = FALSE)
```

## 4. Results

Selected sample sizes (the full table of all `r nrow(results)` sizes is saved in `results/05_cauchy.csv`). For a Cauchy(0, 1), the theory says the median is 0, the IQR is 2, and the share beyond ±10 is `r round(1 - 2 * atan(10) / pi, 3)`, **at every n**:

```{r}
#| label: table
key_n <- c(1, 2, 5, 10, 20, 30, 50, 100)
show  <- results[results$n %in% key_n, c("n", "median", "iqr", "beyond10",
                                         "sim_mean", "sim_sd", "skewness",
                                         "excess_kurtosis")]
knitr::kable(show, digits = 3, row.names = FALSE)
```

## 5. Plots

The sample means from a Cauchy include a few gigantic values, so a normal histogram would be one thin spike. I zoom in on −10 to 10 and say so. The red curve is the **true** distribution of the sample mean (Cauchy(0, 1), which does not change with n). The dashed blue curve is what the CLT would predict if σ were 1: a normal curve that gets narrower like 1/√n.

```{r}
#| label: histograms
show_n <- c(1, 2, 5, 30, 100)
par(mfrow = c(1, length(show_n)))
for (n in show_n) {
  means <- all_means[, as.character(n)]
  h <- hist(means[abs(means) < 10], breaks = seq(-10, 10, by = 0.5), plot = FALSE)
  h$density <- h$counts / (B * 0.5)
  plot(h, freq = FALSE, ylim = c(0, 0.45), col = "gray85", border = "white",
       main = paste("Cauchy(0, 1)\nn =", n), xlab = "Sample mean (zoomed)")
  curve(dcauchy(x), add = TRUE, col = "firebrick", lwd = 3)
  curve(dnorm(x, 0, 1 / sqrt(n)), add = TRUE, col = "steelblue", lwd = 2, lty = 2)
}
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

**Q–Q plots** (points on the red line = normal). Here the y-axis is zoomed to −10 to 10, and the extreme points fly off the chart at every n:

```{r}
#| label: qqplots
par(mfrow = c(1, length(show_n)))
for (n in show_n) {
  means <- all_means[, as.character(n)]
  qqnorm(means, ylim = c(-10, 10), main = paste("Cauchy Q-Q plot\nn =", n))
  qqline(means, col = "firebrick", lwd = 2)
}
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

You can try any n yourself in the [Interactive Sampling Distribution Explorer](https://nprodhuturi.github.io/clt-monte-carlo/interactive/explorer.html).

**Diagnostics across every n.** Unlike the other populations, there is no theory line to approach. The left chart shows the IQR of the sample means, which should shrink if averaging helped; the middle chart shows the share of sample means beyond ±10, which should go to 0 if averaging helped; the right chart shows the simulated SD, which is meaningless for a Cauchy:

```{r}
#| label: diagnostics
par(mfrow = c(1, 3))
plot(results$n, results$iqr, type = "b", pch = 16, cex = 0.6, ylim = c(0, 3),
     xlab = "n", ylab = "IQR of sample means", main = "Spread (IQR)")
abline(h = 2, lty = 2, col = "firebrick")

plot(results$n, results$beyond10, type = "b", pch = 16, cex = 0.6, ylim = c(0, 0.15),
     xlab = "n", ylab = "share beyond +/-10", main = "Extreme sample means")
abline(h = 1 - 2 * atan(10) / pi, lty = 2, col = "firebrick")

plot(results$n, results$sim_sd, type = "b", pch = 16, cex = 0.6, log = "y",
     xlab = "n", ylab = "simulated SD (log scale)", main = "Simulated SD (not meaningful)")
```

## 6. My definition of "approximately normal"

I use the same rule in every analysis. A sample size n counts as approximately normal when **all four** of these hold:

1.  The histogram is bell-shaped and the Q–Q plot is close to the line.
2.  \|skewness\| ≤ 0.25.
3.  \|excess kurtosis\| ≤ 0.5.
4.  The simulated SD is within 5% of the theoretical SE (σ/√n).

My selected n is the smallest n that passes and stays passing for every larger n I tested. The reasons for each cutoff are in [01_standard_normal.md](01_standard_normal.md). For the Cauchy, check 4 cannot be evaluated because σ does not exist, so I judge it with the pictures and the IQR instead.

## 7. Interpretation

```{r}
#| label: interpretation
iqr_lo   <- min(results$iqr)
iqr_hi   <- max(results$iqr)
b_lo     <- min(results$beyond10)
b_hi     <- max(results$beyond10)
sd_1     <- results$sim_sd[results$n == 1]
sd_big   <- max(results$sim_sd)
sd_100   <- results$sim_sd[results$n == 100]
```

- **Shape.** At every n the histogram looks like the same peaked Cauchy curve (red) and never like the narrowing normal curve (dashed blue). The Q–Q plots have the same S-shape at n = 1 and n = 100, with extreme points far off the line.
- **Spread.** The IQR of the sample means stays between `r round(iqr_lo, 2)` and `r round(iqr_hi, 2)` for every n (theory: exactly 2). A normal average would shrink like 1/√n, so at n = 100 the IQR would be about 0.13. It does not shrink at all.
- **Extreme values.** The share of sample means beyond ±10 stays between `r round(b_lo, 3)` and `r round(b_hi, 3)` for every n (theory: `r round(1 - 2 * atan(10) / pi, 3)`). Averaging does not make big values rarer.
- **Mean and SD.** The simulated SD is `r round(sd_1, 1)` at n = 1 and `r round(sd_100, 1)` at n = 100, and its largest value is `r round(sd_big, 1)`. It jumps around and does not settle, because it is dominated by whatever extreme value was drawn. The simulated mean is also unstable for the same reason. These numbers describe the random extremes, not a real mean or SD.
- **Skewness and kurtosis.** The simulated skewness and kurtosis are also erratic, so I do not use them as evidence here. The IQR and tail-share results above are cleaner.

**CLT assumptions.** The CLT needs a finite variance. The Cauchy has none (not even a mean), so the assumption fails, and the conclusion fails with it.

**Limitations / surprises.** The surprise is that more data does not help at all: an average of 100 Cauchy values is just as wild as a single one. A rule that depends on σ (like mine) cannot even be run, so I used the IQR and the tail share instead. The limitation of those two measures is that they check spread and tails but not every part of the shape. The exact result (the mean of n Cauchy(0, 1) values is Cauchy(0, 1)) is the real reason the answer is no.

## 8. Selected n and justification

| **Final answer: no n works** |
|:----------------------------:|

$$\boxed{\text{no } n \text{ works}}$$

- **Evidence.** The IQR stays near 2 (`r round(iqr_lo, 2)` to `r round(iqr_hi, 2)`) instead of shrinking, and the share beyond ±10 stays near `r round(1 - 2 * atan(10) / pi, 3)`. The histogram never narrows toward the dashed normal curve, and the Q–Q plots never straighten.
- **Why no n.** The sample mean of n Cauchy(0, 1) values is exactly Cauchy(0, 1), so no sample size, however large, makes it normal.
- **Is the number 30?** No, and neither is 300 or 3,000. For the Cauchy the answer is that **no number works**, because the CLT assumption of finite variance is broken.
